cultural.vision_reason: This is a Ragamala painting (Bhairavi Ragini) from a Rajput/Indian manuscript tradition depicting a woman worshipping a Shiva-linga — a distinctly Indian Hindu iconographic and stylistic subject, not Khmer art.

physical.title: album
physical.summary: A painting on paper (bound into an album) from the Manley Ragamala (ragamala - lit. 'garland of melodies', and thus a compendium of the musical modes and the emotions associated with them).  This is the 'Bhairavi Ragini'. It depicts a woman with a female attendant worshipping a Śiva-linga, placing garlands on it and chanting, keeping time with the cymbals she holds in her hands.  She sits in a pavillion set in a lake, which is filled with lotuses and water birds. At the base of the linga are various ritual vessels, while a diminutive bull is shown curled up on the pavilion steps. Inscribed.

cultural.vision_reason: This is a European comic sketch of stick-figure skaters in Regency dress, captioned "after Cruikshank" (a named English caricaturist), with English captions like "The Lads that can do it" and "Damn the Dog" — it depicts ice-skating antics in Britain and has no connection to Khmer/Cambodian culture whatsoever.

physical.title: drawing
physical.summary:
Tiny figures, composed of lines, one each for trunk and limbs, with small dots for head, hands, and feet, after Cruikshank, all related to skating. [1] The Lads that can do it', figures skating; [2] 'Attitudes every thing', figures skating striking strange poses, one of them falling; [3] 'Bang up and Bang down', various figures skating towards the right, looking like they are about to fall on their knees; figures at the centre falling, including a figure pushing another on a chair; [4] 'Damn the Dog', a skater tripping over a dog; [5] 'how funny' a skater falling while another laughs; [6] 'Stopping' a figure falling on his back and two at the front stopping abruptly; [7] 'In for it', skaters falling on a hole on the ice; [8] 'Sugar & Brandy up & win en', the wet skaters out of the water talking to a female figure in front of a basket; [9] 'Devilish Cold', two figures felling cold, one hugging himself; [10] 'A race', skaters racing towards the left; [11] 'Mull'd Raspberis', a figure holding a bottle and glass, a jug warming on the left; [12] 'Glass of Good Gin or  slice of good Gingerbread', a figure holding a basket and bottle, a small figure next to the basket and another drinking from a glass; a figure having his skates affixed to the right; [13] ''Have em on hire Sir', a figure holding a skate over a table, two others going towards it to look.
Pen and Ink

cultural.vision_reason: This is a French satirical lithograph from "La Caricature" depicting Louis Philippe and French political figures (Persil, Thiers) in a scene of mutual theft — a work of 19th-century French political art with no connection to Khmer culture.

physical.title: print; satirical print
physical.summary:
Plate 439, No 210: satire representing Louis Philippe hugging an unidentified  man (Robert-Macaire? Guizot?) whilst stealing his wallet, while the latter steals the King's handkerchief; at left, Persil, stealing the man's wallet; and Thiers, grinning, holding a purse; two other figures embracing and stealing each other at right.  13 November 1834
Lithograph
